Chapter One
The Arrival
An arrival more than a century in the making

The gate has been open since 1916.

Before the biography, before the record, before the restoration, there is the feeling of the place itself.

The approach to Garran Hill is unhurried by design. A procession of lawn, drive, trees, and threshold. Long before the door opens, the estate has already begun its introduction.

In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest.

Chapter Two
The Page Provenance
Appointed by Wilson. He held the alliance from London.

Before Garran Hill was an estate, it was an intention.

Walter Hines Page, born in Cary, North Carolina. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Company. Appointed by Woodrow Wilson as Ambassador to the Court of St. James in 1913, and kept there through the years the world came apart.

From London, he bought a hundred acres of Moore County sand and pine. He hired a Boston firm to draw the plans. He sent his son Ralph to supervise the build. Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen, the same men building Pinehurst two miles away, laid the brick under the supervision of J. R. McQueen.

He named it Garran Hill. He never spent a night here.

"The farm. The farm. The farm."Walter Hines Page · from his letters · 1913–1918

Page returned from London in December 1918. His son carried him off the train at Aberdeen. He died ten days later at Currituck Cottage in Pinehurst. He did not return to Garran Hill.

"Well, Frank. I did get here after all, didn't I?"Aberdeen station · December 1918

He is the only American diplomat of the First World War honored with a tablet at Westminster Abbey.

Chapter Three
Built in Bond
The Threshold · 1916

The door has been open since 1916.

Garran Hill, 1916. Inlaid in the threshold stone before ground was ever broken. It has not been altered. It has not been restored. It simply remains.

Full Brick · Flemish Bond · Neo-Georgian

The same craftsmen who built Pinehurst built this house.

Red, handmade, full-bodied brick, laid in the measured rhythm of Flemish bond above a traditional water table. The authority is in the masonry. A house built not for fashion, but for endurance.

The Staircase · 1916

The same curve since 1916.

The mahogany volute turns from the foyer in a single continuous arc. It has been climbed every day, by every person who has lived in this house, since the craftsmen finished it.

Chapter Four
The Rooms
01 / The Salon

A Georgian fireplace. Glass doors to the terrace.

The Salon is the first room of consequence after the foyer. Nearly forty feet from end to end. High ceilings, the Georgian mantelpiece centered on the outside wall, glass doors on both ends.

In the afternoon, the room fills with a quality of light that belongs to the grounds as much as the house.

02 / The Drawing Room

Delft tile. Georgian mantel. A room enlarged for dancing.

They made it bigger so they could dance.

The fire is lit in the frame and the whole room shifts register, from formal to private. Blue walls, white woodwork, a Delft-tiled fireplace surround. It was always meant to be the room you retreat to. The flame holds the center.

Fire going, no one home yet.

03 / The Dining Room

Long table. Dark wood. The chandelier centered above.

The shell cabinets flanking the fireplace are original to the house. The folding screen between the dining room and the hall folds flat and disappears into the wall. It has been doing that since 1916.

The windows face east. Morning light comes in low and direct.

04 / The Library

Floor to ceiling. Three walls deep.

The shelving on three walls holds what was left behind and what was brought in. The rolling ladder runs the full width. The French doors open to the grounds, and in the afternoon the light crosses the floor and reaches the spines on the opposite wall.

This is the room the house was built around. When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

05 / The Kitchen

The kitchen is not original to 1916. It is original to the restoration.

The kitchen was not updated. It was designed.

Heart-pine floors, not the oak of the original rooms. A distinction that tells you exactly what this space is and when it arrived. A wall of windows over the main sink faces grass, magnolias, plane trees, and the pool beyond.

The architectural plans, all fifteen sheets, transfer with the property.

06 / The Powder Room

Mirror. Marble. Ornament that earns its place.

The powder room reads like a jewel box. Floral wallpaper, ornate brass, warm marble underfoot. It is small on purpose. The detail is the point.

Even the smallest rooms carry ceremony.

07 / The Primary Suite

Custom wall panels. A fireplace. Drawn for private life.

The primary suite has a fireplace and custom wall paneling, a first-floor wing taking the full depth of the house. Two dressing rooms, because two people lived here and neither had to wait.

The bath looks straight into the garden. The French doors mean the morning can be private before it is anything else.

Chapter Five
Preserved, Restored, Remembered

Garran Hill carries the rarest kind of restoration. One that renewed the house without taking away its memory.

Not renovated into anonymity. Restored back into itself.

New plumbing, electrical, structural work, climate control, custom Marvin windows. Yet the soul remained intact: seven carved mantels, original oak flooring, leaded-glass sidelights, the arched fanlight, solid-wood doors with brass key plates that still turn.

During restoration, matching the original brick became an act of devotion. The search took three months, because here, even repair had to respect the original hand.

Some rooms were built for company. Some were built for the person who stays after everyone leaves.

Chapter Six
The Hollycrest Years
A private history · 1959–1984

If Page gave the estate its origin, Betty Dumaine gave it its legend.

In 1959, Elizabeth Dumaine purchased the property and renamed it Hollycrest, for the native holly trees near the front of the home. She brought horses to the grounds, and a life organized around animals and land and the particular pleasure of a place that required real attention.

She kept this land for twenty-five years. One horse she buried here. Blue Fox. The stone still stands in the shade of the trees she planted.

Someone still puts flowers there.

My Irish Hunter · Blue Fox

A relic that cannot be staged.

It can only be inherited.

Chapter Seven
The Grounds
4.15 Acres

The house is only the beginning.

The Pool · Salt Water

Through old iron gates, inside brick walls.

The 20 by 40 pool catches afternoon light inside its brick walls. Converted to saltwater in 2022. The brick enclosure dates to the original build. The pool sits within it the way a courtyard sits within a house. Contained, sheltered, belonging.

The Courts · Private

Two lighted courts. They ask for new surfaces and nothing more.

Two regulation courts with commercial-grade fencing and lighting, set under the longleaf pines. The bones are right.

The Wee Cottage

A cottage in the azaleas. Its own complete world.

Built as a children's playhouse. Its own architecture, its own scale, its own silence. A small house within the larger story, on the same four and fifteen-hundredths acres.

Chapter Eight
The Last Parcel

The land was sold in pieces. The house was not.

A subdivision rose around it and took the name. The house kept the rest. The brick, the forest, the four acres that were always its own.

The last piece of Garran Hill on its own ground.
